sections:
Under the Screen

The long bones

Under the screen the bones of the arm and thigh show a second shadow inside the first, as if a heavier bone waited folded within the lighter one.

Fluoroscopy shows a denser inner cortex within each long bone: the second form's skeleton, held compressed.

The skull

The face is a man's, but the jaw is hinged further back than any man's, and the teeth are set deep for a longer row.

The mandibular joint sits posterior to the human norm; unerupted canines lie deep in the bone.

The sinews

The ligaments are knotted in two places where one would do, so that they can let go and take hold again.

Each major ligament carries a second anchorage, used when the skeleton lengthens.

The Account

The Lycanthrope is a man by day and a wolf by the full moon, and the change is no spell he casts but a weight he carries, which the moon draws up through his bones.

A Grafted human body carrying a dense inherited form from below, which the full moon's pull releases as a violent skeletal change into Chimeric flesh.

O

Of the wolf-man there are as many accounts as there are moors. Ovid tells of Lycaon, a king of Arcadia, who served human flesh to Jupiter and was turned into a wolf for it, keeping his grey hair and his savage look. The Romans told of a soldier who stripped by the tombs on a bright night, made water around his clothes, and ran off howling; the clothes had turned to stone. The Bretons call him bisclavret, the Normans garwaf, and the shepherds of every country between have a name for him and a story to go with it.

Of his kinds the Registry counts one, though it shows two faces. By day and through most of the month he is a man, and passes for one, though he runs hot, sleeps badly, and is restless when the moon fattens. At the full he is something else: taller, heavier, long in the jaw, and without the man’s mind to govern him.

He is found where people are few: on moors, at the forest’s edge, in the hill country. He is solitary by necessity, for a man who is a wolf one night in thirty soon learns to live where he will not be missed.

Of his body this much is certain: the wolf is not put on him from outside. It is in him already, folded inside his bones like a second skeleton, and the moon draws it out as it draws the sea. The change is not a melting but a breaking. The long bones crack and lengthen, the sinews tear and catch again, and the face is pulled forward into a muzzle. Those who have watched it say it is the sound they remember.

He is not to be pitied without care, nor feared without reason. The man may be gentle; the wolf is not anything at all but hunger. The old remedies are practical ones. Keep him from the full moon behind a strong door, and keep his clothes, for in the oldest tales the man returns to his shape only by them.

Body: human for most of the lunar month, with a dormant second form in the bone and connective tissue. Source: the Second Tier, inherited. Trigger: the full moon, when the illuminated fraction passes about 0.97; extreme strain (a fall, a fight, a sudden run) can start a partial change at any phase. Mechanism: the skeleton remodels in minutes. Bone thickens and lengthens, ligaments tear and re-anchor, the skull draws out into a muzzle. The change is not chosen and is not reversible until the moon wanes. Containment: restraint through the night; old accounts keep the clothes, since the return to human form goes by them. Hazard to the observer: severe, during the change and for the night that follows.

Its Habits

The specimen is quiet under a slow eye. A reader who rushes down the page puts it under strain, and the bones give way into the wolf until the reading slows again.A fast descent through the page is read as strain: the skeleton shatters into the dense form and settles back when the reading rests.

On a night when the reader's own moon is full, the theatre opens on the wolf, and it is the man who must be looked for beneath.When the moon is at least 0.97 illuminated for the reader, the room opens in the transformed state and the lens shows the human skeleton instead.

Read slowly and the man stays a man. Both shapes are drawn side by side for any reader who asks for stillness.Paging quickly by keyboard counts as strain; a fling does the same by touch. With reduced motion the two states are shown as still plates.

  • The wolf, as the full moon or the strain leaves it, hunched under the glass.Transformed state. Long bones extended, skull drawn into a muzzle.

Exemplars

How the Lycanthrope has been shown, truly and falsely. Those that wore the wrong name are set out first.Portrayals filed under this entity. Rejected labels first, then the reference portrayals.

  1. AnomalyUnclassified

    Jacob Black in New Moon

    Stephenie Meyer, 2006 · book · called “werewolf”

    Jacob Black is entered as an anomaly near the Lycanthropes, for the moon has no hold on him: his change is his own to make, and it was first set loose by the nearness of an enemy.Jacob Black is an anomaly because his transformation is voluntary and was first triggered by the presence of vampires, not by the moon, so he fits none of the sixteen.

  2. True to its nameLabel confirmedModel exampleReference portrayal

    David Kessler in An American Werewolf in London

    John Landis, 1981 · film · called “werewolf”

    David Kessler is the model of the Lycanthrope, for the bite on the moor puts the wolf in him and the full moon breaks him open bone by bone.David Kessler is the model Lycanthrope because a bite transmits the condition and the full moon forces a long, painful restructuring of the skeleton.

  3. True to its nameLabel confirmedRunner-upSecondary reference

    Remus Lupin in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban

    J. K. Rowling, 1999 · book · called “werewolf”

    Remus Lupin stands second among the Lycanthropes, a gentle scholar bitten as a child who must give himself up to the wolf at every full moon.Remus Lupin is the runner-up Lycanthrope because a childhood bite left him with a change forced by every full moon, which a potion can tame but not prevent.

Its Nearest Neighbour

The Kitsune. The fox also changes its shape, but the fox chooses, and grows wiser by it. The wolf is changed, and every change is a breaking.Kitsune shape-change is voluntary and cumulative. Lycanthrope change is forced by the moon and is skeletal trauma.
